meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.

meanings.note: Softens a statement or downplays a motive.

examples.trans: I just asked out of curiosity.
I'll just stay home today.

나가다.gloss: to go out, to step outside

meanings.en: to go out, to step outside, to leave a room
meanings.note: 나- ('out') + 가다 ('to go')

examples.trans: Let's step outside for a moment and talk.
He went out of the conference room.

meanings.en: to be dying of (hyperbolic emphasis in -아/어 죽겠다)

examples.trans: I'm starving to death.
It's so hot I feel like I'm going to die.

meanings.note: Takes a complement marked with 이/가.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.
It has already become 12 o'clock.

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.
Because I think I'm late.

meanings.note: Used in -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 to express 'it seems that...' or 'I think...'.

meanings.en: to be the same, to be like
meanings.note: Compares two things with -와/과 같다.

examples.trans: I think I'm late.
It looks like it's going to rain.
Do you have time today?
Where are you going?

meanings.note: Used only with close friends, younger people, or children

examples.trans: Did you hear about this drinks or something?
I was busy today because of drinks or something.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for eating a meal or food; honorific equivalent is 드시다.

examples.trans: Let's eat lunch together.
Did you eat breakfast?

meanings.note: interrogative pronoun; becomes 누가 before subject particle -가
indefinite pronoun

examples.trans: Did someone come outside?
Who is that person?

meanings.note: Used when repeating an action.

examples.trans: See you again!
It is raining again.

meanings.en: to fight; to quarrel; to argue
meanings.note: The opponent takes -와/과 or -랑.

examples.trans: Do you fight with your younger sibling often?
Don't fight with each other and get along.

meanings.note: Determiner modifying a following noun.

examples.text: 그런 실수는 누구나 할 수 있어요.
examples.trans: Anyone can make a mistake like that.
This is the first time I'm hearing a story like that.

examples.text: 그동안 차갑게만 보이던 내 이미지를 친근하게 바꾸려는 거야.
examples.trans: I am going to change my cold image into something friendly and approachable.

examples.text: 이 신발은 너무 신경 쓴 것 같잖아, 털털한 이미지인데.
examples.trans: These shoes look like I tried too hard when I am going for an easygoing image.
Please give me some water.
Please wait just a moment.

meanings.note: Contraction of 조금

그렇다.gloss: to be so, to do so

meanings.en: to be like that, to be so
meanings.note: ㅎ-irregular; also used as a pro-verb ('do so / say so')

examples.trans: Is that really so?
Don't keep acting like that.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adv).

examples.text: 아무래도 미래의 의사다 보니까 공부할 것도 많고.
examples.trans: Well, since I am a future doctor, I have a ton of studying to do.
Here the word for 'after all, naturally' is key.
Did you hear about this yesterday?
I was busy today because of yesterday.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 그냥 어제를 내 인생에서 확 도려내버리고 싶다.
examples.trans: I just want to carve yesterday right out of my life.
Here the word for 'from my life' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (adv).

examples.text: 그냥 어제를 내 인생에서 확 도려내버리고 싶다.
examples.trans: I just want to carve yesterday right out of my life.
Here the word for 'in one clean sweep' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 그냥 어제를 내 인생에서 확 도려내버리고 싶다.
examples.trans: I just want to carve yesterday right out of my life.
This expression comes from 'carve completely out'.

meanings.note: Auxiliary adjective attached to a verb stem with -고 (-고 싶다).

examples.trans: I want to go to Korea.
I want to drink a cup of coffee.
It really is is loud, so compared to what I thought.
Especially today, it is is loud, so and nice.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 크게 싸웠구나, 합의금 물어줘야 되고 그래?
examples.trans: Must have been a huge fight—do you have to pay settlement money or something?
Here the word for 'settlement money' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 크게 싸웠구나, 합의금 물어줘야 되고 그래?
examples.trans: Must have been a huge fight—do you have to pay settlement money or something?
This expression comes from 'must compensate'.

그러다.gloss: to say so; to do so

meanings.en: to say so; to speak like that
meanings.note: contracted from 그러하다; often follows quoted speech

meanings.en: to do so; to act like that

examples.trans: Who said that?
That friend also said they are going together.

meanings.note: Colloquial spoken form of 너희네; used among close friends or to juniors.

examples.text: 너네 오늘 수업 몇 시에 끝나?
examples.trans: What time does your class end today?
You guys all come over here together.

meanings.note: dummy

examples.trans: dummy trans 1
dummy trans 2

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 너네 팀이 종이 타러 가면 행정반에서 별소리 안 하고 주지?
examples.trans: When your team goes to pick up paper, the admin desk hands it over without a fuss, right?
Here the word for 'paper' is key.

meanings.note: intransitive verb; also means 'to ride' in another sense

examples.text: 불을 줄이지 않으면 고기가 다 타요.
examples.trans: If you don't lower the heat, the meat will burn completely.
Firewood is burning brightly in the stove.

meanings.note: Basic verb of motion. With the respectful ending -세요 in 안녕히 가세요, it forms the polite farewell 'Goodbye!'. RR: gada.

examples.trans: I am going home.
Go safely!

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 너네 팀이 종이 타러 가면 행정반에서 별소리 안 하고 주지?
examples.trans: When your team goes to pick up paper, the admin desk hands it over without a fuss, right?
Here the word for 'at the admin supply desk' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 너네 팀이 종이 타러 가면 행정반에서 별소리 안 하고 주지?
examples.trans: When your team goes to pick up paper, the admin desk hands it over without a fuss, right?
Here the word for 'complaints, fuss' is key.

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

examples.trans: I'm not going to the office today.
I haven't watched that movie yet.

meanings.en: to do, to perform, to hold
meanings.note: Core verb; also combines with nouns to form verbs.

examples.trans: What are you doing right now?
We are holding a meeting today.

meanings.note: Used for giving things to someone of equal or lower status.

examples.trans: I gave a gift.
Please give me some water.
Did you hear about this problem?
I was busy today because of problem.
What time is it now?
I'll leave right now.

meanings.note: 1st person plural pronoun; also used for 'my' with family, school, or workplace

examples.trans: Our team has a good atmosphere.
Let's eat lunch together tomorrow.

meanings.note: Combines with 하다 in 말하다 (to speak, to say).

examples.trans: I don't know what you mean.
You speak Korean well.

좋다.gloss: to be good, to be nice

examples.trans: I feel really good today.
It's nice to take a walk in the morning.

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Goodbye! (to someone leaving)

meanings.note: Honorific equivalent of 있다; used in 안녕히 계세요 ('goodbye' to someone staying).

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Is the teacher inside right now?
